island.e: From earlier iland, from Middle English iland, yland, ylond, from Old English īeġland, from Proto-West Germanic *auwjuland, from Proto-Germanic *awjōlandą (from Proto-Germanic *awjō (“island, waterland, meadow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂) + *landą (“land”), equivalent to ey + land.
island.g: A contiguous area of land, smaller than a continent, totally surrounded by water.

islander.g: A person who lives on an island.

isle.e: From Middle English ile, yle (with s added, similar to English island), borrowed from Old French ille, idle, isle, from Latin insula. Not related to island.
isle.g: An island, usually very small. Compare with islet.

isolate.e: Back-formation from isolated, from French isolé, from Italian isolato, from Latin īnsulātus (whence also insulate), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).
isolate.g: To set apart or cut off from others.

isolated.e: A rendering into English of French isolé.
isolated.g: Placed or standing apart or alone; in isolation.

isolation.e: From French isolation, from isolé, placed on an island (thus away from other people). Equivalent to isolate + -ion.
isolation.g: The state of being isolated, detached, or separated; the state of being away from other people.

issue.e: From Middle English issue, from Old French issue (“an exit, a way out”), feminine past participle of issir (“to exit”), from Latin exeō (“go out, exit”), from prefix ex- (“out”) + eō (“go”).
issue.g: The action or an instance of flowing or coming out, an outflow
